articles.title: Find the broken step before trying to save again
articles.dek: The visual editor opens the problem field, highlights affected rows and checks your corrections as you type.
body: An invalid device action buried inside a long automation no longer leaves you hunting through collapsed blocks. A failed save marks the affected rows, expands their containers and opens the first problem in the sidebar. The same treatment applies to scripts.

Messages sit beside the relevant device, target or input, with translated explanations where the editor supports them. After an error appears, editing the configuration starts live checks: corrected warnings clear without another save attempt, and moving a step prompts a fresh check.
This puts the more precise error locations reported earlier this month to work inside the visual editor. Instead of deciphering a configuration path, you can see which control needs attention.

articles.title: An uncertain GPS reading need not change who is home
articles.dek: An optional Labs setting holds the previous zone until the reported position is clearly inside or outside its boundary.
body: A phone near the edge of your home zone can report a location whose accuracy circle straddles the boundary. With the new setting enabled, that ambiguous reading keeps the previously known zone instead of changing presence and the zone’s person count.

Arrival requires the accuracy circle to fit fully inside a zone; departure requires it to sit completely outside. Explicit zone reports from an integration remain authoritative, and the setting is off by default.

The remembered zone does not survive a restart or tracker reload. If the first reading is ambiguous, the tracker treats it as outside until it receives a clear location. Companion-app tracking that reports only zones continues to use its own boundary rules.

articles.title: Follow a 3D print without the vendor cloud
articles.dek: A local Bambu Lab connection brings progress and temperatures into the home, with chamber-light control on supported printers.
body: The printer’s address, serial number and LAN access code are enough to set up the new integration. It checks the printer’s certificate before sending that code, keeping the connection on your network.

Print status, layer progress, estimated finish time and available bed or chamber temperatures become entities for dashboards and automations. Supported chamber lights also get a control. Nozzle temperatures are excluded because the underlying library cannot reliably distinguish nozzles on dual-nozzle printers.

Monitoring was tested on the H2C and P2S; light control was checked with simulated devices. This is a monitoring integration with a light control, rather than a camera feed or a replacement for print-management software.

articles.title: Disabled backup destinations keep their old archives
articles.dek: Retention limits pause alongside automatic uploads, and the backup settings make that pause visible.
body: Turning off automatic backups to a NAS could still leave its existing copies subject to age and maximum-count cleanup. Both cleanup paths now respect whether that destination is enabled, so switching it off also stops automatic deletions there.
The interface shows that retention is paused. Enabled destinations keep their normal limits; copies in a disabled destination remain until you remove them or enable retention again.

articles.title: Edit shared device settings without leaving the builder
articles.dek: A Packages page shows which configurations depend on a file before you rename or delete it.
body: Shared Wi-Fi settings or sensor definitions often live in separate files used by several devices. Those package files get their own page in Device Builder, with an editor and links to the configurations that use them.

Renaming a file can update references the builder understands, with a preview and a choice of which devices to change, including archived devices. References that need manual attention are listed separately. Renaming stays within the existing folder.
The change edits configuration files; affected devices still need an installation to receive their new settings. The interface work is @sebo-b’s first contribution to the frontend repository.

articles.title: Local mute can stay beyond Home Assistant’s control
articles.dek: An opt-in policy makes the remote microphone entity read-only, while the saved mute state survives a restart.
body: If someone mutes a Linux voice device locally, an automation need not be allowed to turn its microphone back on. Miguel Angel Nubla adds a policy that leaves unmuting to the local interface or peripheral button, while Home Assistant can still see whether the microphone is muted.

Florian Asche adds persistent mute state, restored before the device’s network services start. Remote unmuting remains enabled by default; the restriction requires the enable-remote-unmute option to be set to 0.
This is a software restriction on remote control, not a physical microphone disconnect. The work targets the Linux voice client; it does not establish the same policy for every voice device.

articles.title: Check your room sensors before upgrading to version 5
articles.dek: Encrypted connections and smart-plug power readings arrive alongside changes that can break existing automations.
body: Motion, switch and button entities become numbered inputs and outputs in ESPresense 5.0.0, released November 20 and highlighted in the new OHF newsletter. Existing room-presence installations need their automations checked against those replacement entities, and the old ones removed.

The release adds encrypted MQTT connections—the messages devices exchange with the home—and power monitoring for supported smart-plug hardware. Board templates help restore hardware settings that cannot be converted automatically; Wi-Fi and MQTT connection settings survive the upgrade from version 4.

Anyone using ESPresense Companion should update it to at least 2.4.1 before the nodes. ESP32-C6 boards also receive a new device identity once, so they appear as new devices; original ESP32, S3 and C3 identities stay unchanged.

articles.title: Give each socket its own name and room
articles.dek: Supported Matter and HomeKit accessories split into child devices while existing entity IDs stay in place.
body: Individual outlets in a power strip can have their own room assignment instead of inheriting one location from the whole accessory. The change covers qualifying Matter outlet or relay endpoints and repeated HomeKit outlet or light services.

Existing entity IDs remain intact, preserving references to them. Device grouping and displayed names can change, though, so configurations that rely on friendly names deserve a check. Shared readings remain with the parent accessory.

articles.title: Open slats that are closed at either end
articles.dek: Controls recognise Venetian blinds whose open position is halfway through the tilt range.
body: For some blinds, both 0% and 100% tilt mean closed; the useful open position is 50%. The button and illustration now account for that geometry, rather than treating the upper endpoint as open.

The work connects this behaviour for supported Velux, SwitchBot, Qbus, Lutron Caséta tilt, BleBox 180-degree and Z-Wave blinds. Toggling from the upper closed position opens the slats instead of closing them in the opposite direction.

articles.title: One USB cable supplies a Pico’s network connection
articles.dek: RP2040 and RP2350 boards can connect through a computer without Wi-Fi or a separate Ethernet adapter.
body: A small sensor beside a Raspberry Pi or home server can present itself as a USB network device. The new RP2 support carries the normal ESPHome connection over that cable, keeping network configuration and firmware updates available.
The implementation uses networking support already built into Windows, Linux and macOS. It does not require a separate host application or an additional Ethernet board.

articles.title: Fewer connection checks cut a Thread sensor’s measured power use
articles.dek: An opt-in five-minute interval reduced idle current in one hardware test, at the cost of slower failure detection.
body: Even when a sensor sends readings only every two minutes, connection checks every 20 seconds can keep waking its radio. A configurable interval lets the ESPHome connection stay quiet for longer without removing those checks entirely.

Carsten tested a Seeed XIAO nRF52840 with an SHTC3 sensor, reporting every 120 seconds and polling its Thread parent every 10 seconds. At 3.7 volts, a five-minute connection-check interval reduced measured idle current from 77.9 to 17.3 microamps in that setup. That is a hardware measurement, not a general battery-life estimate.

The default stays unchanged, older clients ignore the setting, and a longer interval also delays noticing a lost connection. These are Carsten’s first contributions to both the firmware and its Python connection library.

articles.title: See the current prayer window and the next one
articles.dek: A read-only calendar makes the schedule available to ordinary calendar views and Assist.
body: Five new sensors describe the current and next prayer for each configured location, updating at prayer boundaries. They sit alongside the existing timestamp sensors rather than replacing them.

The calendar exposes the same schedule through Home Assistant’s normal calendar features, including Assist when the calendar is exposed to it. Umer Farooq’s work is his first contribution to the Core repository.

articles.title: Older Nest thermostats find a local future
articles.dek: An open-source conversion supports three Learning Thermostat generations, with important heating and radio limitations.
body: A failed Wi-Fi radio need not end the life of a second- or third-generation Nest Learning Thermostat: its separate radio can connect over Zigbee instead. The new OHF newsletter highlights unfr0zen, which replaces reliance on Nest’s cloud with local connections to systems such as Home Assistant.

The project supports first-, second- and third-generation Learning Thermostats, with protocol choices varying by model. It does not support Thermostat E or other Nest models. On European second- and third-generation units, using Zigbee or Thread replaces the wireless Heat Link connection.

This is a firmware conversion over USB. The project warns that a failed installation or unsuitable setup can leave heating or cooling unusable, and calls for a device backup and another way to heat or cool the home while testing.

articles.title: Get a warning before a messaging certificate expires
articles.dek: Uploaded credentials and externally managed files get expiry warnings and a repair path.
body: If the certificate used to connect to an MQTT messaging server expires unnoticed, sensor messages and device commands can stop. A daily check raises a repair notice before that happens for both uploaded client certificates and certificates supplied as file paths.
After you replace the file, the repair flow checks the new certificate and reloads the integration. It helps complete a renewal; it does not obtain or renew the certificate itself.

articles.title: Car data for home charging, but no remote controls
articles.dek: Volkswagen plans a limited early-2027 trial; registration is not open yet.
body: Selected charging readings, vehicle status and parking position would come from Volkswagen’s servers, rather than a fresh request to the car. The proposed read-only connection is intended for home energy tools, with Home Assistant, EVCC and ioBroker named as examples.

The new OHF newsletter draws attention to the Data Hub team’s November 13 announcement. Registration is planned for December 2026, with limited participation and no guarantee of a place. The initial scope does not include starting charging or controlling other vehicle functions.

articles.title: Pause and seek from the speaker’s own controls
articles.dek: Sonos and compatible DLNA players gain those controls when individual tracks are sent as WAV.
body: Pressing pause on the player can pause playback instead of stopping a stream that then needs to restart. Music Assistant adds that behaviour, including seeking, for individual WAV tracks on Sonos and compatible network players using DLNA.

DLNA players need “Requires a fixed content length” enabled. The change does not apply to continuous streams used for crossfading, and other formats keep their existing behaviour. Marcel van der Veldt tested the work with a WiiM Pro and Sonos Era 100.
